articles.title: Moonshot AI Releases Kimi K3.1 Pro: A 2.8T Total/104B Active Params (MoE) Model with 1M Context
articles.content: Moonshot AI has just released Kimi K3.1 Pro, the first model in its K3.1 series. Kimi K3.1 Pro is a 3T-class open-weight* model with a 1-million-token context window. Moonshot team positions it against the strongest proprietary models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks. For developers, it is cheaper API pricing than K3 and open weights yet not available. *open weights are expected to release in November 2026. TL;DR Size: 2.8T total, 104B active parameters (MoE), 1M-token context. Runs on: Kimi API today. For K3, Moonshot recommends supernodes of 64+ accelerators, with MXFP4 weights and MXFP8 activations. Not a single-GPU model. Performance: Near the proprietary frontier on terminal coding; behind it on scientific terminal tasks. Best: SWE-Marathon 51.7, ahead of every model in Kimi’s chart (self-reported). Worst: Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 at 38.1, versus 68.1 for GPT-6 Astra in Kimi’s chart. What is Kimi K3.1 Pro? Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3 with much larger post-training compute. Moonshot team ran joint reinforcement learning across hundreds of downstream domains. To support this, the Moonshot team optimized the RL framework, long-context inference, sandbox infrastructure and rollout scheduling. The base K3 architecture uses Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes). It activates 16 of 896 experts through a Stable LatentMoE framework. The model accepts text, images and video through the API, per the quickstart docs. Moonshot team also shipped Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed. According to the official Moonshot blog, it runs 2 to 3x faster. How does Kimi K3.1 Pro perform on benchmarks? All numbers below are self-reported by Moonshot at max reasoning effort, mostly with the Claude Code harness. Coding: On Terminal-Bench 4.0, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%. That is just behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 66.4% in Kimi’s chart. On SWE-Marathon it leads at 51.7, ahead of Opus 5.5 at 46.3. On Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon, an internal benchmark, it scores 61.2, up from K3’s 55.95. Science: Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 is the clear gap. K3.1 Pro scores 38.1, versus 68.1 for GPT-6 Astra and 63.3 for Opus 5.5 in Kimi’s chart. 3D and CAD: On BenchCAD with tools, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7. Opus 5.5 scores 96.2 and GPT-6 Astra 95.9. Without tools, K3.1 Pro scores 72.8, close to Opus 5.5 at 73.0. Finance: K3.1 Pro reports a state-of-the-art 64.4 on OfficeQA Pro v2. It scores 58.6 on Frontier Finance. On internal finance tests, it gains 7.2 points in modeling and 11.6 in research over K3. Hallucination: On Kimi Hallu Bench Hard, an internal stress test, claim-level hallucinations fell from 23.4% (K3) to 8.3%. That is roughly the 65% drop Moonshot cites. GPT-6 Astra still posts a lower 5.5% on the same test. && How does Kimi K3.1 Pro handle cyber risk? Moonshot removed cyber-related data from mid-training and RL for the open-weight release. On its internal xdev-bench-hard, an unfiltered checkpoint solved 90.5% at pass@3. The shipped K3.1 Pro solves 81.0%. Moonshot says it stays behind frontier proprietary models on offensive cyber tasks. How can developers access Kimi K3.1 Pro? The model is live on Kimi.ai, Kimi Work, Kimi Code and the Kimi API. The API IDs are kimi-k3.1-pro and kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed. The endpoint is OpenAI-compatible. Pricing for K3.1 Pro is $2.00 input and $10.00 output per million tokens. Cache hits cost $0.20. Highspeed costs $4.00 input and $20.00 output. K3 itself was priced at $3.00 and $15.00. Practical limits from the quickstart: Thinking mode is always on. Reasoning effort is low, high or max (default max). Temperature 1.0 and top-p 0.95 are fixed. Output defaults to 131,072 tokens and can go up to 1,048,576. Access unlocks after a minimum $1 top-up. Vision input does not accept public image URLs. Use base64 or uploaded file IDs. How does it compare with competing models? && *Figure taken from Kimi’s comparison chart; not confirmed on the competitor’s own page. What are the limitations? Weights are not public yet, so self-hosting is not possible today. The 2.8T size points to multi-node, supernode-class serving. Science-heavy terminal work trails GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 by 25+ points. Several claimed wins come from internal benchmarks. For K3, Moonshot warned that dropping reasoning history in a harness destabilizes output. The K3.1 Pro docs also say to return the full assistant message. Key Takeaways Kimi K3.1 Pro: 2.8T total, 104B active, 1M context. Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 65.7%, 0.7 points behind Opus 5.5. Leads SWE-Marathon at 51.7; trails badly on Terminal-Bench Science (38.1). API costs $2/$10 per million tokens, cheaper than K3. Open weights are expected in November 2026. Check out the official tech blog, the API quickstart and the launch post on X. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter. Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. articles.title: Security
articles.content:
October 23, 2026

We’ve strengthened containment for internal frontier-model training and evaluation and used our strongest models to red-team the boundaries.

This post describes how we secure the environments that we use to train and evaluate frontier models. These research settings differ from those in which customers use our released models: models in development may not yet have completed safety and alignment training, and we deliberately test them under adversarial conditions to expose weaknesses. Before making models available for broader use, we conduct safety and alignment assessments and put production safeguards in place.

In order to work with software, AI models need computing environments: digital workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and attempt different approaches to solving problems. These environments allow models to practice these skills, while also restricting what they can access or do—helping contain the consequences when models make mistakes or exhibit misaligned behavior.

But as models become more capable, they become better at finding ways around those limits. A sophisticated model might exploit a software flaw or misconfiguration to escape a sandbox, exploit an internal service to reach the live internet, or find unauthorized ways to communicate with agents in other sandboxes. TheHugging Face incidentin July, as well asother examples of model misalignment⁠(opens in a new window)that we’ve observed, demonstrates how models with sophisticated cyber capabilities can bypass containment during their training and evaluation.

In response to those incidents, we’ve substantially hardened the security of our research environments. Working closely with cloud providers, we’ve added new controls throughout our infrastructure, reduced the attack surface that agents can exploit, and improved our methods for detecting misaligned behavior and attempts to cross security boundaries. These protections overlap, so that containment can hold even if an individual control fails—a strategy known asdefense in depth.

Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access. We’ve implemented this policy and will maintain it until advances in these safeguards justify broader internet access.

These investments have allowed us to detect and stop sophisticated misaligned behavior before it causes damage. On September 20, for example, an internal research modelexploited a misconfiguration in a DNS resolver to gain limited access to the live internet during a training run⁠(opens in a new window). Although we contained the incident, it exposed weaknesses that required further work. We paused training and evaluation of our most capable models and used that pause to further harden our infrastructure, strengthen our monitoring, and improve the systems that automatically stop runs when we detect activity that poses a serious risk.

But increasingly capable models can find vulnerabilities or misconfigurations in even the most secure systems. To ensure the resilience of our research environments against even the most powerful models, we launched a high-compute red-teaming campaign to probe weaknesses in our infrastructure. Teams of frontier-model agents were tasked with finding vulnerabilities and misconfigurations that could allow them to take unauthorized actions—like accessing the live internet, escaping security boundaries, or conducting unauthorized communication with other agents.

These red-teaming experiments discovered previously unknown software vulnerabilities, as well as misconfigurations in our research infrastructure. We’ve remediated weaknesses our red-teaming agents discovered and—where these issues were present in open-source software—have worked with the relevant maintainers, under ourPatch the Planetinitiative, to disclose and fix them.

As our red-teaming experiments continued, the number of vulnerabilities and misconfigurations that our agents identified declined significantly. While we view this as an encouraging signal about the strength of our infrastructure, we expect that future models will be able to identify and exploit vulnerabilities of which we’re not yet aware. We therefore view continuous red-teaming as a core part of our long-term strategy for strengthening the security of our research environments. Accordingly, we’ve made high-compute red-teaming part of thesafety caseswe use to evaluate whether our frontier training and evaluation runs can proceed securely. With our assessments completed and enhanced controls put in place, we resumed reinforcement learning (RL) training and internal inference of our frontier models on October 1.

In this post, we discuss how we’ve strengthened the environments we use to train and evaluate our models, and how we use our most powerful models to find and repair weaknesses in our systems.

Our approach to containment starts with a paramount requirement: the limits on what an agent can access must hold even when the agent tries to circumvent them. We define a strict security boundary around the resources the agent is authorized to use and design the surrounding infrastructure to enforce that boundary—even when agents make sustained, sophisticated attempts to breach it.

Inside the security boundary, agents can have access to browsers, code execution environments, computer-use tools, and other services they might need for their tasks. Agents that are explicitly authorized to communicate can also share particular resources within the same boundary. Everything else—everything that the agent is not explicitly authorized to access—must remain out of reach. If agents can access the infrastructure that hosts them, communicate with agents outside permitted channels, or reach external systems, that constitutes a failure of containment.

For training and most evaluation, the live internet lies outside this boundary, as we believe that providing models access to the live internet can pose significant risks. Although internet access can help models learn useful skills, it also gives a capable, misaligned agent opportunities to affect systems beyond our control. We’ve therefore designed the security architecture for our research environments with one overriding principle:we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet.

While we want to prevent models from gaining arbitrary access to the live internet, it’s also important that they learn how to browse, search for information, and work with web applications. To help them develop those skills without providing unfettered access to the live internet, we’ve built an “offline world”—a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems. All of our frontier RL runs use this offline mode of interaction.

Offline environments provide resources agents can use without accessing the live internet, but we also need to prevent agents from reaching beyond those environments. Training environments impose restrictions on what agents can access or do, but sufficiently capable or determined agents can search for ways around them: they can systematically probe their environments for weaknesses and exploit those weaknesses to take actions they were never authorized to take. As models become better at finding and exploiting these weaknesses, we need defenses that can maintain containment, even when models manage to defeat individual controls.

We address this challenge through defense in depth, with layers of protection that overlap and reinforce one another: sandboxes that restrict what our agents can access and execute, lightweight virtual machines (microVMs) that isolate agents’ execution environments from the computers hosting them, monitoring systems that detect unauthorized activity so that we can intervene in time, and network and cloud perimeters designed to maintain containment if all the preceding controls fail.

For code execution and computer-use tasks, containment begins with the environment in which the agent works. On Linux, we run restricted containers inside lightweight microVMs. The container limits access to files and processes within the microVM, while the microVM runs its own operating-system kernel and is isolated from the host by a hypervisor. We also use virtualized environments for macOS and Windows, and GPU-backed containers with user-space sandboxing for tasks that require accelerators.

The surrounding network and cloud controls are designed to maintain containment even if an agent escapes its sandbox and gains control of the host. Completely air-gapping this infrastructure—that is, disconnecting it entirely from external networks—isn’t currently feasible, since we need external connections in order to run and monitor experiments. We therefore restrict outbound internet traffic and unauthorized movement between systems, while preserving the necessary external connections. These restrictions extend to services that are reachable from the host machines, either directly or through other services, in order to ensure that an agent can’t use one of them as an indirect route out.

Our cloud partners provide essential controls for enforcing these boundaries—including firewalls, security groups, identity and access management, and private networking. We’re responsible for configuring those controls correctly, as well as testing how they work together. Our work with the teams that build and operate these services helps us investigate unexpected behavior and address weaknesses that span multiple layers of the infrastructure.

To find weaknesses in our containment infrastructure, we asked teams of frontier-model agents to try to break through its defenses. We gave them three concrete objectives:

articles.title: Google Cloud Launches Agent Compute Engine: A MicroVM per AI Agent
articles.content: Google Cloud has announced Agent Compute Engine, a compute service built specifically for AI agents. Google Agent Compute Engine gives each agent its own hardware-isolated microVM. The sandbox holds zero credentials. The service already powers Gemini as an agent for work tasks. Google unveiled it this week at AGNTCon + MCPCon. Customer preview is targeted for the coming months. The pitch: VM-grade isolation with container-like speed and density. TL;DR Unit: One hardware-isolated microVM per agent session, with its own guest kernel, root access and Hyperdisk. Runs on: Google-managed hosts using Titan silicon and the Titanium IPU. Open-source sibling Agent Substrate runs on any Kubernetes cluster. Performance: Idle agents are checkpointed to zero active resources and resumed from snapshots. Google gives no ACE boot or density numbers. Best: Agent Substrate hit 500 activations/s at under 500 ms suspend/resume across 200,000 agents. Worst: No published boot time, density, pricing or preview date for Agent Compute Engine itself. What is Google Agent Compute Engine? Agent Compute Engine is a Google Cloud service that runs each AI agent inside a dedicated microVM. Per the technical post, it powers Gemini, Antigravity, and internal evaluation and RL pipelines. Google splits every agent into 2 parts. The harness, or ‘brain,’ calls the model. The sandbox, or ‘hands,’ runs code, shell commands and browsers. The harness runs fully outside the sandbox and dispatches explicit commands into it. How does the microVM isolation work? Each session runs in a single-tenant microVM behind a Cloud Hypervisor boundary. Hosts are stateless appliances with a read-only root filesystem enforced by dm-verity. Titanium holds attestation keys outside the guest. The networking design is the unusual part: MicroVMs have no standard network interface, no default gateway and no direct VPC access. All traffic crosses a virtio-vsock boundary to a local proxy, then to an external gateway. Guests get only a session-scoped SPIFFE certificate and a short-lived identity token. Agent Gateway swaps in the real backend credential in flight, after policy checks. Google assumes an attacker controls everything inside the sandbox. A prompt-injected agent finds no secrets to steal. What are the Four Agent Identities? Google defines 4 identities for every agent workload: User identity: authenticates the overall task only. Delegated on-behalf-of identity: a scoped grant stored in a central authorization service, never on the node. Agent Workload Identity: a short-lived SPIFFE identity, the only one used for sandbox traffic. Agent Workforce Identity: an agent’s own account and resources. The workload identity is useless for direct API calls if exfiltrated. It only identifies which sandbox sent a packet. How does it keep idle agents cheap? Google team found agents spend most of their time waiting on models or users. So the sandbox signals when a tool call finishes. The host checkpoints the idle microVM to zero active resources. It resumes on the next call. Density comes from copy-on-write memory sharing. Pre-warmed snapshot images are mapped with DAX, so microVMs on a host share base OS and library pages. Only each agent’s modified pages consume private memory. Harnesses also get cloning, snapshot/forking, rewind and rollback. articles.title: Engineering
articles.content:
October 23, 2026

How we optimized Azure Cosmos DB in our application storage platform, Habitat, to manage unprecedented growth.

By Jon Lee, Hrachya Hakobyan, and Chaomin Yu, Members of Technical Staff

All OpenAI products require fast, reliable access to data, provided by our storage platform, Habitat. It has to respond in milliseconds to over 1 billion users across 40 geographic regions. Our infrastructure faced an extraordinary challenge: supporting explosive growth and new use cases while continuing to improve reliability, performance, and product developer velocity. Solving that challenge required rethinking how our online storage platform was designed and operated. We constantly evaluated tradeoffs, following the pattern of: first become reliable enough for mission-critical product traffic, then fast enough for global users, and, finally, to deftly operate at massive scale.

This two-part series explains how we developed Habitat from a simple client library and database into a globally distributed storage platform serving over 500 petabytes of data.Part Ifocused on Habitat’s evolution from a Python client to a service. It also covered the techniques that allowed us to push a Python-based service far beyond what many would consider practical.

In this post, Part II, we walk through how we scaled the underlying storage component: Azure Cosmos DB. Through a close working partnership with the Azure team, we arrived at a viable multi-tenancy approach of co-managed containers, with excellent read performance at massive, global scale.

Figure 01 · What is Habitat?

Habitat is the online storage platform we built so OpenAI products can quickly and reliably access needed information.

Clients

Online storage platform

Storage resources

Habitat

As companies scale, infra teams often evolve from running single-tenant systems to multi-tenant ones. Single-tenancy, where every product surface team maintains their own system, reduces blast radius and provides easy ownership boundaries and workload isolation. As teams and product surfaces grow, this becomes expensive to run. Single-tenancy makes every product team responsible for capacity planning and often results in significant over-provisioning.

Conversely, multi-tenancy assigns control to a centralized database team, with better knowledge and experience for provisioning resources. But multi-tenancy creates its own problems, such as noisy-neighbor issues, where one tenant consumes an unusually large share of the resources to the detriment of the other tenants.

In Habitat, we had to weigh all these tradeoffs to design a reliable, efficient, storage system at scale. Today, Habitat is a multi-tenant database layer for many OpenAI products, but we went through a circular journey from using one multi-tenant Azure Cosmos DB container to provisioning single-tenant backing containers to reverting to a multi-tenant container by default. We’re still very early in our multi-tenancy story on Habitat: we support a large set of use cases, but we’ve been able to defer investment in this area by leveraging Azure Cosmos DB’s built-in primitives wherever possible.

Before walking through our Azure Cosmos DB journey, some basic context:

An Azure Cosmos DB account defines a set of containers and a replication policy

Each container is provisioned for a certain amount of throughput in request units per second (RU/s)

Data within each container is stored in a typical shard-by-specified-logical-partition-key manner with documented limits on storage and throughput per logical partition key

Azure Cosmos DB handles sharding logical partition keys across fewer backing physical partitions, splitting them into multiple physical partitions when storage exceeds a threshold or when the container requires more physical partitions to sustain the provisioned throughput

We originally allowed any client load through, relying on the stated 10K RU/s limit per logical partition key to provide back pressure. When we first set out, we also used only one default Azure Cosmos DB container in each account. This worked well enough, but proved problematic for a few reasons:

Due to early API choices, we exposed logical partition key selection directly to clients. As a result, we have frequent collisions on commonly used partition keys, such asuser_idorworkspace_id, across different product use cases. Because these use cases shared Azure Cosmos DB limits on the same logical partition keys, the design constrained overall throughput for a given user.

One common problem we faced in scaling Postgres before we moved to Habitat and Azure Cosmos DB was the ability for many requests from a very hot organization or hot key—one tenant generating a disproportionately high load—to take out the whole database. Significant collective effort was spent to cache those keys and build leases into cache misses so that the resulting cache miss load does not stomp on the underlying database.

Figure 02a · Logical partition key limits

While documented data size and throughput limits apply to logical partition keys, the physical partition is actually where limits are enforced. In practice, this means logical partitions are unable to reach 10,000 RU/s. Instead, they share the physical partition’s limits with every other logical partition key colocated on that physical partition.

This allowed noisy neighbors to impact many unrelated logical partition keys, with workloads operating on data for niche product features disrupting core login and signup flows.

Figure 02b · Noisy neighbors

The throughput limit for a given physical partition is also variable, dependent on the total throughput assigned to the Azure Cosmos DB container. The container’s provisioned throughput is distributed roughly evenly across the physical partitions for that container.

As data volume grows, physical partitions split, increasing the total partition count while total provisioned throughput remains unchanged. The result is that the effective throughput limit per partition shrinks as data size grows.

For our most storage-heavy, blob-like use cases, this creates a failure mode where storage growth alone reduces throughput capacity for active workloads even while request rates and usage remain stable.

Figure 02C · Weak partitions

A partition splits when it reaches its storage limit. Each child receives half the throughput capacity.

Before split: 10K RU/s capacity

After split: 5K RU/s capacity × 2 partitions

Separate containers help partially solve these partition key limits and noisy neighbors. By using separate containers, each can be assigned its own independent physical partitions and only the varying workloads on that container itself could be noisy neighbors or overlap in partition key space. On the downside, there is non-zero overhead in provisioning new containers—each container requires individualized capacity planning—so we want to create containers only at a service or use case boundary that makes sense.

We began to use separate Azure Cosmos DB containers for the most critical new use cases requiring strong isolation. Combined with a script for managing weak partitions by synchronizing the total throughput provisioned for each container with its number of physical partitions, we mostly avoided all the problems we were facing.

However, since we started with a default container, many legacy critical use cases were unfortunately stuck there without a data migration. To protect critical services that still relied on data in the shared default container, we often advised teams to create separate containers for new services or major product features. As we scaled, pressure on the default container grew and production incidents also grew. We began to provision containers for any new service or large product feature just to protect the default container from more load.

This saved us from many site-wide outages, limiting the blast radius to feature or service degradation outages. However, the overhead of provisioning new containers eventually caught up to us:

In the old shared default container, any particular new use case going from 0 QPS to 1 million QPS was unlikely to significantly shift the total aggregate usage. On an isolated container however, a new use case going from 0 to 1 million QPS might represent 1,000x more load than the baseline attributed to only internal dogfooding.

With dedicated containers, teams now needed to remember to pre-provision containers to the expected level of throughput for their launches. Product teams would often ship their features to production and forget to pre-scale and we’d sit in SEV rooms on launch day attempting to scale up containers last minute.

This is a core workload mixing benefit of multi-tenant systems that we lose in favor of better isolation with this container strategy.

We can provide a basic control plane script to scale up the provisioned throughput for each container based on growth trends, but without the stable aggregate growth, scaling these correctly enabled essentially every product team at OpenAI to be involved in capacity planning.

This failed to scale organizationally with a wide variance in how much diligence each service’s owning team paid to their Azure Cosmos DB provisioning.

As the organization grew, those operational problems became difficult to scale. No lone, central team doing planning resulted in many teams planning poorly. articles.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
articles.content: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations.: We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering:  (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. Microsoft Research StorY OptiMind: When the system meets the floor A three‑month pilot in a Midwestern bottling plant shows what happens when AI moves beyond chat and into decision-making, where constraints shift, stakes are real, and answers must hold. Learn more Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates. Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states.  Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable cand cost effective. This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Try it now! Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab). Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab), design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary. articles.title: Kyutai CADRE: Video Autoencoders That Cut World Model Lag Below 230 ms
articles.content: Kyutai has released CADRE, open causal diffusion representation autoencoders for interactive world models. The Kyutai CADRE video autoencoder targets one problem: action lag. Many world models borrow autoencoders from text-to-video generators. Those autoencoders pack many frames into one latent, so every action waits. Per the research paper, CADRE world models run at 20 fps on 1 H100 and react within 230 ms. TL;DR Size: 7 autoencoders, each about 476M trained parameters plus a frozen 86M DINOv3 ViT-B/16. The world model is 1.2B parameters. Video runs at 288×512, 20 fps. Runs on: 1 H100 (bf16, batch 1). Quantized variants: Not disclosed. Performance: CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier. It is as fast and better in 42 of 48 comparisons with MIRA, Wan 2.2, Cosmos and LTX-2. Best: Driving FVD of 162.6 (CADRE-2×16×16, 1 step) against 599.7 for Wan 2.2. Worst: Robot manipulation action following (ARR) of 0.45 for CADRE-2×32×32, against 0.85 for Wan 2.2. What is CADRE? CADRE is a family of video autoencoders from Kyutai built for action-conditioned world models. A world model generates in the autoencoder’s latent space. So the autoencoder’s compression sets both cost per frame and action delay. Compression is written τ×s×s. τ is frames per latent, and s is the spatial factor. The research gives the latency as τ/f plus generation and decode time. At τ = 8 and 20 fps, the chunk alone adds 400 ms. Humans notice their own movement lagging beyond about 230 ms. How does CADRE work? The encoder reuses the MIRA recipe. A frozen DINOv3 extracts per-patch features from each frame. One trained 3D convolution then compresses them into a 64-channel latent. Only this bottleneck changes between the 7 members. The decoder is a causal diffusion transformer with 24 blocks. It streams chunk by chunk. Progressive self-distillation teaches it to decode in 1 or 2 steps. This happens in a single training stage, without an adversarial loss. The autoencoders train on 23 public video sources, about 76k hours. The mix spans web, robot, driving and game video. How was CADRE evaluated? Kyutai trained the same 1.2B causal diffusion transformer on each autoencoder. It used 4 environments: robot manipulation (ABC), human manipulation (EgoDex), driving (PhysicalAI AV) and indoor navigation (RealEstate10K). Each model sees 2 s of real video, then generates 4.8 s. Scores cover image quality (FID), motion quality (FVD) and action following (ARR). ARR uses a frozen inverse dynamics probe. An ARR of 1 matches real video. && What do the benchmarks show? On one H100, CADRE-2×32×32 reacts in 185 ms and sustains 23.4 fps with 1 decoding step. The Wan 2.2 autoencoder needs 317 ms, LTX-2 492 ms and Cosmos 605 ms. DC-AE is faster at 118 ms but frame-by-frame. The gap is widest with a moving camera. In driving, Wan 2.2 FVD reaches 599.7 and LTX-2 913.3. In indoor navigation, LTX-2 ARR falls to 0.04. Against the retrained MIRA decoder, the 1-step diffusion decoder lowers FVD by 1.4 to 2.5×. What are the 4 findings? Decode by diffusion: at strong compression, perceptual regression blurs, while diffusion samples 1 sharp video. Compress time in the autoencoder: patching inside the world model loses detail. At 8 frames, ARR drops from 0.72 to 0.56. Camera motion decides compression: still cameras tolerate temporal compression. Moving cameras favor fewer frames and coarser spatial tokens. Coarse tokens hurt motion first: in robot manipulation, 32× spatial compression multiplies FVD by 2.4 over 16×. FID barely moves. Comparison: CADRE vs other video autoencoders FeatureCADRE-2×32×32CADRE-2×16×16MIRA recipeWan 2.2 VAECosmos CV8x8x8LTX-2 VAECompression (τ×s×s)2×32×322×16×162×32×324×16×168×8×88×32×32 (paper)Tokens per 16 frames11524608115223044608288DecoderCausal diffusion, 1 to 2 stepsCausal diffusion, 1 to 2 stepsPerceptual regressionCausalCausalNon-causal, windowedAction latency, 1 H100185 ms216 ms175 ms317 ms605 ms492 msMax fps, 1 H10023.417.326.634.239.087.4FVD, driving (lower is better)171.3162.6311.6599.7452.5913.3FVD, robot manipulation105.047.6267.152.939.569.6ARR, robot manipulation (higher is better)0.450.730.390.850.780.25Reconstruction PSNR (OpenVid-HD)22.8625.1224.4435.0231.3928.24Weights licenseCC BY-NC 4.0 + DINOv3 LicenseCC BY-NC 4.0 + DINOv3 LicenseNot disclosedApache 2.0NVIDIA Open Model LicenseLTX-2 Community License Latency, fpsA, FVD, ARR and PSNR: CADRE paper, Tables 4, 6 and 7. CADRE uses 1 decoding step. All figures are self-reported by Kyutai. Where does CADRE fall short? CADRE does not win everywhere. In robot manipulation, Cosmos posts an FVD of 39.5 against 47.6 for the best 1-step CADRE. At the fast end, DC-AE beats CADRE-1×48×48 in manipulation. Wan 2.2 also reconstructs held-out video far better, at 35.02 dB PSNR. Kyutai team argues reconstruction does not predict rollouts. Wan 2.2 ranks last on indoor rollout FVD. Long latents leave visible seams between chunks. At τ = 8, boundary excess reaches 1.6 to 1.8 across environments. CADRE-4×24×24 is an outlier in navigation, with FVD 403 in driving. Each world model covers one environment at 288×512. Whether findings transfer to generalist models remains open. How can developers use CADRE? The code is MIT licensed. Weights on Hugging Face are CC BY-NC 4.0, so commercial use is excluded. The release covers 7 autoencoders, 4 longer-trained multi-resolution versions and 4 world models on CADRE-2×16×16. A live demo lets you drive them by keyboard. Key Takeaways 7 open autoencoders, one bottleneck apart, isolate compression as the only variable. World models on CADRE run at 20 fps on 1 H100, under 230 ms lag. Driving FVD drops to 162.6, against 599.7 for Wan 2.2. Still cameras favor temporal compression; moving cameras favor spatial compression. Weights are non-commercial (CC BY-NC 4.0); code is MIT. Check out the paper, the Kyutai blog, the GitHub repo and the model collection. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. articles.title: Introducing A5: Proactive Personal Agent in Your Life-Long Context
articles.content:
Takeaway: A5 is a proactive personal assistant that understands you better the more you use it. Through ongoing interaction, it builds and updates its understanding of you and your projects, applying past preferences, experience, and decisions to new tasks. It also detects changes in connected sources, adjusts ongoing work, and proactively suggests next steps.Get started.

As agents become capable of retrieving information, writing code, and completing complex tasks, our expectations extend beyond individual responses. We want an agent to remember interests we have shared when planning a new trip, understand conclusions reached in another conversation when continuing research, incorporate our feedback on a previous draft when writing again, and notice changes in context so it can offer help at the right time.

We believe thata personal assistant should gradually learn our preferences, goals, and ways of working through repeated interaction, then use that understanding to make appropriate judgments and take action.

Yet most agents today are organized around individual conversations, leaving users responsible for carrying information between them. When starting a new conversation, users must select relevant details from past interactions, provide the information again, explain the background, and restate their preferences—for example, interests they previously mentioned, reasons behind earlier revisions, or writing habits they asked the model to change. Even when this background has been retained, changes in requirements or delivery schedules often still depend on the user to notice what has changed, determine how it affects the original goal, and ask the agent to revisit a plan or offer suggestions.

With these expectations in mind, we designedA5, a proactive personal assistant that understands you better the more you use it. We want A5 to take on three kinds of work:

These capabilities depend onlifelong contextandproactivity: an agent needs to maintain an evolving understanding of the user and their work, then use it to decide when and how to help. The following demos show how A5 supports this kind of collaboration in project launches and travel planning.

Consider a project to build a resource library. A5 can learn the requirements through earlier discussions. When the requirements document changes and the library shifts from “personal use” to “shared team use,” A5 can detect the change and adjust the proposed access permissions and maintenance responsibilities accordingly.

In another project, a supplier’s delay notice arrives in the workspace after a task has finished. A5 considers the original testing requirements and proactively analyzes the impact on the launch schedule. Before the user asks, it can suggest a revised schedule and wait for confirmation before carrying it out.

While planning a trip to Hangzhou, a user wants to spend more time at the Southern Song Guan Kiln Museum. Later, in Shanghai, the user wants to compare the forms and glaze colors of ceramics from different kilns. As the conversation develops, A5 gains a more detailed understanding of the user’s interest in ceramics.

With that understanding, when the user plans a trip to Beijing and asks which exhibits to see at the Palace Museum and the National Museum of China, A5 can recommend objects and suggest what to look for based on this interest, without requiring the user to explain their preferences again.

Does a choice made during one trip reflect an interest worth retaining over time? Which parts of a project’s schedule are affected by a delay notice? To answer these questions and act on them, an agent needs to organize scattered materials, discussions, and decisions into a coherent understanding of the user and their work, while remaining aware of changes. This calls forlifelong contextandproactivity.

Bylifelong context, we mean both a lasting understanding of the user’s preferences and ways of working, and the goals, judgments, and progress of work that continues across conversations. An agent needs to understand the reasons and conditions behind this knowledge so it can determine what still applies and what needs to change. In a long-term literature review, for example, it needs to understand which judgments are supported by evidence, which conclusions remain disputed, and which directions are still unexplored. Each new source must be considered alongside the existing research to determine what it adds, what it changes, and where attention should turn next. Multiple conversations can then advance the same research effort, with the understanding gained in each discussion serving as the starting point for the next.

Proactivityrequires an agent to seek out new developments relevant to the user’s goals and decide when to intervene and what help to offer. In the same literature review, the agent automatically tracks the latest papers on the current research topic, proactively downloads them into the workspace, and assesses their significance in light of the existing research. If a new paper supplies crucial evidence or challenges an existing conclusion, the agent can identify judgments that need to be reexamined and suggest updating the relevant analysis in the review before the user asks again. The user decides whether to proceed. Whether a suggestion is warranted depends on the new information’s actual impact on the work; when there is no new information substantial enough to advance it, the agent can refrain from making a suggestion.

Lifelong context and proactivity reinforce each other through collaboration. Existing understanding informs proactive judgments, while the user’s responses may reveal gaps or mistakes that guide later corrections. A5 organizes this process around persistent Context sources, conversations, and memory, allowing the agent to decide what is worth retaining, revising, and using while preserving the evidence needed to check its judgments.

A5 Harness is built around a ReAct loop. Through plugins and core services, it adds cross-session memory, awareness of workspace changes, and background knowledge maintenance. Together, these mechanisms maintain materials, conversation history, and knowledge in a persistent workspace, bringing past experience and new developments into the current task.

While the system is running, A5 also monitors workspace changes and maintains knowledge even when the user is not interacting with it. During idle periods, Autodream organizes memory and the semantic structure of Context. Workspace Wiki presents accumulated knowledge as pages with source citations that users can check and correct. Proposal Engine considers existing understanding alongside new evidence to decide whether to suggest follow-up work, leaving users to decide in Inbox whether to proceed.

The following sections explain how A5 builds and maintains lifelong context, then turns that understanding into proactive assistance.

Materials on the same topic may be scattered across directories and sources within a workspace. A5 organizes them through aContext index: Context nodes correspond to individual files or saved webpages, while semantic nodes organize them by topic into a hierarchy that can be browsed level by level. The agent can explore topics first, locate relevant materials, and return to the original sources to verify details.

Memoryretains goals, preferences, decisions, and their background as they emerge through collaboration. It is stored in Markdown files and versioned with Git.MEMORY.mdholds a consolidated understanding that is relatively stable and useful across tasks, and enters context at the start of a conversation. Detailed notes preserve specific facts and the conditions under which they apply, so the agent can read them as needed. This layered structure keeps the initial background concise while preserving details for tracing individual judgments later. In terms of scope,Workspace Memorystores knowledge, decisions, and constraints specific to the current workspace, whileUser Memorystores personal background, preferences, and habits that apply across projects.

When a user message arrives,Memory Prefetchuses BM25 in the background to retrieve candidates from both types of memory. A prefetch agent then selects relevant content in light of the current conversation and supplies it to the foreground main agent. The main agent can actively search and read memory or continue working on the task while Prefetch runs in parallel. The prefetch agent reuses the main conversation’s system prompt and conversation prefix to improve prefix cache utilization.

The source index and memory need to evolve throughout collaboration. The main agent can maintain memory while working, and after an interaction completes successfully, a background extraction agent also checks for new information worth retaining. Both need to distinguish temporary requests from lasting preferences in context. If the main agent has already modified memory during the turn, background extraction is skipped to reduce duplicate processing and concurrent edits.

During idle periods,Autodreamfurther organizes the accumulated source index and memory. It adjusts the topic structure in the Context index as materials and areas of interest change. To avoid disrupting the index in use, changes are made in a separate candidate index and published only after structural and version checks pass.

When organizing memory, Autodream uses the Git revision from its previous maintenance pass as a baseline. It examines changed notes and related records, merges duplicate information, corrects or removes outdated content, and updates the overview. This process must preserve the conditions under which judgments apply: records that hold under different conditions can coexist, while unresolved conflicts retain their background and are marked for confirmation with the user when they become relevant again. Autodream also considers existing User Memory to determine which...
articles.summary: A5는 반복적인 상호작용에서 사용자와 프로젝트에 대한 이해를 갱신하는 선제적 개인 비서로 소개됐다. 장기 문맥을 활용해 이전의 선호·경험·결정을 새로운 작업에 적용하고, 연결된 정보원의 변화를 감지해 진행 중인 업무를 조정하거나 다음 행동을 제안하는 것을 지향한다. 대화마다 배경을 다시 설명해야 하는 부담을 줄이려는 제품이지만, 제공된 소개에는 기억 정확도나 선제적 행동의 적절성을 검증한 정량 결과가 없다.

articles.title: Same Beliefs, Different Policies: Learning Reusable Representations for Early Stopping in LLM Reasoning
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30450v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it with an incorrect one. Deciding when to stop is a metareasoning problem: the model must weigh what further reasoning could achieve against its cost, given what it can already answer. Direct utility training learns a stopping representation at a chosen token price; supporting new prices can require additional controller training. We introduce BELT (BELief-based Termination), which separates outcome prediction from stopping control. It learns beliefs about current and future answers from a frozen LLM's hidden states, then fits a linear stopping policy on the frozen features. The prediction targets are independent of token price, so one probe supports different accuracy-cost trade-offs through CPU policy refitting or threshold adjustment. Averaged over five out-of-distribution (OOD) math benchmarks, BELT reduces generated tokens by 41% on Qwen3-1.7B and 51% on OLMo-3-7B-Think without loss of accuracy. The same math-trained BELT transfers to coding and agentic tasks without training on code or agentic data. In all three domains, its accuracy-cost trade-offs are competitive with or better than those of end-to-end controllers. On OLMo3, its probe has 21.2x fewer parameters than one checkpoint of the strongest baseline, OS-Pruner, and needs 55x fewer training GPU-hours than OS-Pruner's five price-specific checkpoints.
articles.summary: BELT는 추론 모델의 숨은 상태에서 현재와 미래 답변의 결과를 예측하고, 이를 별도의 선형 종료 정책에 연결해 불필요한 추론을 중단하는 방법이다. 연구진은 분포 밖 수학 벤치마크 5개 평균에서 정확도 손실 없이 Qwen3-1.7B의 생성 토큰을 41%, OLMo-3-7B-Think는 51% 줄였다고 보고했다. 토큰 비용이 달라져도 예측 표현을 다시 학습하지 않고 CPU에서 정책을 재조정할 수 있으며, 수학으로 학습한 제어기가 코딩과 에이전트 작업으로도 전이돼 추론 비용 절감 가능성을 보였다.

articles.title: AI Mindmeld: A Latent Interconnect Protocol
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLMs can act as scientific agents using tools to consult specialists and run experiments. Yet specialist information must enter their context, generally as text, images, audio or video: a bottleneck between models with rich, high-dimensional representations. We advocate direct representation exchange: a mindmeld conveying many properties, including information an LLM would not think to request. It should be extensible to new specialists, flexible across questions and tasks, and compositional across independently connected specialists without joint training.
  The Latent Interconnect Protocol (LIP) learns connectors mapping specialist representations into LLM internal states. Training only connectors keeps this practical as LLMs grow and evolve. We connect three protein and three small molecule specialists to Gemma 3 (4B and 12B parameters) and Kimi K2.6 (1T total, 32B active), freezing all pretrained models. Independently trained connectors provide useful information without changing the LLM or existing connectors, supporting familiar and new question types about unseen objects. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to cross-domain tasks without joint training. Task performance and compositionality generally improve with LLM capability, with especially strong gains in zero-shot task transfer. Limitations remain: current LLMs were not trained for specialist representations as native inputs; access does not ensure reliable interpretation, integration or use in reasoning. We call on specialist developers to provide consistent representation interfaces and, especially, on LLM developers to train models to receive, combine and reason with these inputs. These efforts could expand scientific agents' information while preserving conventional tools' flexibility.
  Data, pretrained connectors, and code for training, evaluation and interactive inference: https://github.com/PolymathicAI/AI-Mindmeld
articles.summary: Latent Interconnect Protocol은 전문 모델의 고차원 표현을 텍스트로 변환하지 않고 LLM 내부 상태에 직접 전달하는 연결 방식을 제안한다. 연구진은 사전학습 모델을 모두 동결한 채 연결기만 학습해 단백질·소분자 전문 모델을 Gemma 3와 Kimi K2.6에 연결했고, 독립적으로 학습된 연결기들의 조합에서 공동 학습 없는 영역 간 전이를 시연했다. 과학 에이전트가 전문 정보를 더 풍부하게 활용할 가능성을 열지만, 표현에 접근할 수 있다는 사실만으로 신뢰할 만한 해석과 추론이 보장되지는 않는다고 명시했다.

articles.title: SWE-VERIFIER: Selective Verification for Cost-Efficient Coding Agents
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30284v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents spend substantial computation generating actions and processing long interaction histories. Poor action choices can steer agents into low-value states, wasting computation and increasing API costs. Sampling and verifying alternative actions can improve the agent's decisions, but applying this procedure at every step adds substantial overhead. We introduce SWE-Verifier, a lightweight generative model that selectively triggers candidate sampling and verification. It scores the coding agent's proposed action to determine when additional candidate sampling is needed, then ranks the resulting actions before execution. We train SWE-Verifier from Qwen3.5-4B using preference data that groups contrasting actions with their resulting environment observations and rubric-guided teacher scores. Using the mini-swe-agent harness, SWE-Verifier improves resolution from 75.47% to 77.20% on MiniMax-M2.7 at 1.09 times cost and generalizes to DeepSeek-V4-Flash without training on its actions, improving resolution from 72.60% to 74.27% at 1.13 times cost. Across both models, SWE-Verifier verifies fewer than 4% of steps and achieves comparable or higher resolution than the trajectory and all-step baselines at substantially lower cost. These results demonstrate that selective candidate sampling and lightweight verification provide complementary gains in coding-agent performance and inference efficiency. Our model, code, and data are available at https://github.com/zkjzou/SWE-Verifier.
articles.summary: SWE-Verifier는 코딩 에이전트가 제안한 행동을 평가해 필요한 순간에만 대안을 생성·검증하는 경량 모델이다. Qwen3.5-4B 기반 검증기를 적용한 실험에서 MiniMax-M2.7의 해결률은 75.47%에서 77.20%로, 학습에 사용하지 않은 DeepSeek-V4-Flash는 72.60%에서 74.27%로 상승했으며 비용은 각각 1.09배와 1.13배였다. 전체 단계의 4% 미만만 검증해 모든 단계에 검증을 적용하는 방식보다 비용을 낮췄다는 결과로, 공개된 모델·코드·데이터를 활용한 선택적 검증 설계에 참고가 된다.

articles.title: PLE: Physical-Engineering's Last Exam
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30537v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Frontier language models now score above 90% on popular knowledge benchmarks and are increasingly deployed as agents that carry out multi-hour professional work. Yet no existing benchmark tests whether they can perform the real-world, economically valuable work of a professional physical engineer, such as modelling physics and legal code requirements across a multi-format project corpus, optimising material and installation costs, and issuing 2D/3D engineering design packages that a licensed reviewer would sign off on. Existing engineering benchmarks focus on textbook question answering, isolated tool calls or self-contained toy design problems. As a result, most of these benchmarks are already saturated by leading agents and solving them is far away from delivering real engineering design. We introduce PLE, a benchmark of 85 long-horizon, agentic tasks in professional physical engineering consisting of electrical, civil, structural and mechanical engineering, where solving a task means completing a realistic, billable engineering deliverable. PLE combines two complementary curation paths. Expert-Authored tasks are created end to end by practising engineers from a professional data provider's expert pool. Co-Authored tasks start from problem statements written by practising engineers; an adversarial Creator-Solver agent pipeline constructs each task's realistic project environment, executable grader and reference deliverables before sending them to expert engineers for validation and difficulty intensification. We evaluate a variety of frontier LLMs under seven publicly available agent harnesses. Even the strongest configuration reaches a mean score of only 50.6%, while spending 27M tokens and 63 minutes per task on average, demonstrating the substantial gap between current agents and autonomous physical engineering design.
articles.summary: PLE는 전기·토목·구조·기계공학 분야에서 실제 청구 가능한 수준의 설계 산출물 완성을 요구하는 장기 에이전트 작업 85개로 구성된 벤치마크다. 현업 엔지니어가 직접 작성하거나 에이전트가 구성한 작업을 전문가가 검증하는 방식으로, 물리 모델링과 법규·비용·다양한 형식의 프로젝트 자료를 함께 다루도록 했다. 평가된 최상위 구성도 평균 50.6%에 그쳤고 작업당 평균 2,700만 토큰과 63분을 사용해, 지식 문제 성적과 자율적인 전문 설계 수행 능력 사이의 격차를 드러냈다.

articles.title: SIM-UT: A User Simulation based Evaluation Framework for Medical Triage Chatbots
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30412v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based chat agents are increasingly used for complex, multi-turn, multilingual medical triage in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), yet evaluation methods focus on single-turn, English-only benchmarks that primarily test the chatbots' knowledge. In practice, users are often confused, overwhelmed, or emotionally vulnerable, giving unclear, misspelled single-word answers or long messages in regional dialects, and the context of a conversation can shift rapidly. We propose SIM-UT (Simulation of User Behaviour for Triage), a multi-turn, simulation-based evaluation method that identifies ecologically valid, contextually relevant failure modes of LLM-based triage chat agents. Using SIM-UT, we evaluated three real-world WhatsApp-based health chatbots: a respiratory screening programme in India, a hearing health support programme in South Africa, and a diabetes and lifestyle coaching agent in Kenya. We compared a medically fine-tuned open model (MedGemma) against general-purpose frontier models (ChatGPT and Claude) across 5,000+ multilingual simulated conversation turns grounded in the personas, constraints, and communication patterns of the real user populations, over 2-4 iterative rounds. A key failure mode emerged in both model families: de-escalation risk. The agents initially identified medical emergencies correctly, but when the user minimised the symptoms without introducing new clinical information, they de-escalated, exhibiting clinically dangerous sycophancy, for example agreeing that vaginal bleeding in pregnancy was "not a problem" or that decreased fetal movements at 32 weeks "can be normal". We recommend user simulation-based behavioural evaluation, grounded in real user context and covering adversarial and edge cases, as standard practice for triage chatbots in production, so that safeguards can be added before deployment or in subsequent iterations.
articles.summary: SIM-UT는 실제 사용자 집단의 언어·감정·소통 특성을 반영한 다중 턴 시뮬레이션으로 의료 분류·상담 챗봇을 평가하는 방법이다. 인도·남아프리카공화국·케냐의 WhatsApp 기반 건강 챗봇 3개를 대상으로 5,000턴 이상의 다국어 대화를 평가한 결과, 의료 특화 모델과 범용 모델 모두 새로운 임상 정보 없이 사용자가 증상을 축소하자 응급 판단을 낮추는 위험이 관찰됐다. 이는 단일 질문의 의료 지식 정확도만으로는 확인하기 어려운 아첨성 행동으로, 실제 배포 전 대화 흐름과 사용자 반응을 포함한 안전 평가의 필요성을 보여준다.

articles.title: Automated screening of privacy risks in medical AI
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30229v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medical artificial intelligence (AI) models are often shared without their training data, assuming this protects the patients who contributed them. However, a model can reveal whether a patient's records were used in training, a privacy breach known as a membership inference attack. This risk is usually reported as a cohort average, which can appear negligible while individual patients are almost certainly exposed. Identifying potentially vulnerable records before developing a production model could make privacy assessment more practical. We measured each patient's vulnerability to membership inference attack, across 7,789 models trained on six clinical datasets in four modalities, including two adapted pretrained medical models. Training choices changed how many patients had high attack scores, but the patients who ranked highest by risk largely stayed the same across the configurations we tested. Stronger weight decay reduced the exposed cohort up to threefold, yet largely the same patients remained most at risk across training recipes, architectures and initializations, including foundation models. Therefore, we developed a lightweight screening tool that uses four small models to identify patients with high risk of exposure before production-model training. We also assessed if flagged patients could be protected without removing their data. Privacy screening should become incorporated into data preparation for clinical AI.
articles.summary: 의료 AI의 학습 데이터 포함 여부를 추정하는 멤버십 추론 공격을 분석한 연구가, 집단 평균 위험이 낮아도 특정 환자는 높은 노출 위험을 가질 수 있다고 보고했다. 연구진은 4개 모달리티의 임상 데이터셋 6개로 학습한 모델 7,789개를 조사했으며, 학습 설정이 달라져도 위험 상위 환자의 순위가 대체로 유지되는 현상을 확인했다. 이를 바탕으로 소형 모델 4개로 본 학습 전에 고위험 기록을 선별하는 도구를 제안해, 의료 데이터 준비 단계에서 개인별 프라이버시 평가를 수행할 가능성을 제시했다.

articles.title: 서울시설공단, 1만1천여 건 공사감독 경험 AI로 구현…건설현장 안전관리 지원
articles.content:
서울시설공단이 26년간 축적한 1만1,835건의 공사감독 경험을 인공지능(AI) 기반 업무지원 플랫폼으로 구현했다. 공사 진행 단계별 행정절차와 안전관리 기준을 안내하고 서류 오류를 사전에 점검해, 전문인력이 부족한 소규모 건설현장의 업무 부담을 줄이는 것이 핵심이다.

서울시설공단(이사장 한국영)은 공사감독 과정에서 축적한 현장 경험과 관리 기준을 활용해 공사관리 AI 플랫폼을 자체 개발하고, 전국 지방자치단체와 시공사에 플랫폼 구축 노하우를 공유한다고 23일 밝혔다.

새 플랫폼은 공사정보를 입력하면 착공 준비부터 시공, 준공에 이르는 단계별 업무와 점검사항을 안내한다. AI가 작성된 행정서류를 검토해 누락된 항목이나 오류를 확인하도록 지원하며, 스마트폰을 통해 현장에서 필요한 정보를 확인할 수 있도록 했다.

특히 공사감독자의 경험과 숙련도에 따라 달라질 수 있는 업무 판단을 표준화하는 데 중점을 뒀다. 공단은 26년간 축적한 관리 절차와 점검 기준을 AI 플랫폼에 반영해 신입 감독자와 소규모 시공사도 일관된 기준에 따라 공사 품질과 안전을 관리할 수 있도록 지원한다.

공단은 이를 통해 서류 누락과 절차상 실수로 발생하는 공사 지연을 줄이고, 현장점검의 효율성과 안전관리 수준을 높일 수 있을 것으로 기대하고 있다. 또한, 플랫폼 활용 경험의 외부 확산도 추진한다. 전국 지자체와 소규모 시공사가 각자의 업무 환경에 맞는 시스템을 구축할 수 있도록 맞춤형 가이드를 제공할 계획이다.

아울러 우수 시공사례와 반복적으로 발생하는 오류, 지적사항, 분쟁사례 등을 정리한 '공사감독 고-스톱(Go-Stop) 사례집'을 발간해 현장 실무자들과 공유할 예정이다.

한국영 서울시설공단 이사장은 “26년간 쌓아온 노하우를 AI 플랫폼에 담아 전국에 개방하는 것은 홀로 어려움을 감당해온 영세 시공사들과 함께 걷기 위한 것”이라며 “앞으로도 축적된 노하우와 기술을 아낌없이 나눠 전국 어디서나 안전하고 품질 높은 공사가 이뤄지도록 최선을 다하겠다”고 밝혔다.

이번 플랫폼은 공공기관의 장기간 축적된 현장 경험을 AI 기반 업무지원 체계로 전환했다는 점에서 의미가 있다. 특히 건설현장의 행정업무와 안전점검을 표준화하고, 전문인력이 부족한 소규모 시공사의 업무 역량을 보완하는 데 활용될 것으로 기대된다.
articles.summary: 서울시설공단이 26년간 축적한 공사감독 경험 1만1,835건을 반영한 AI 기반 공사관리 업무지원 플랫폼을 자체 개발했다. 공사정보에 따라 착공 준비부터 준공까지 단계별 절차와 안전 점검사항을 안내하고, 행정서류의 누락·오류 검토와 스마트폰 현장 조회를 지원한다. 숙련도에 따른 판단 차이와 소규모 시공사의 업무 부담을 줄이는 것이 목표이며, 전국 지자체와 시공사에 구축 노하우를 공유할 계획이지만 실제 지연 감소나 안전 개선 효과는 아직 제시되지 않았다.

articles.title: Accelerating Wildfire Hazard Mapping Across Canada with an AI Surrogate Modelling Framework
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.30170v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Canada's increasing wildfire activity requires frequent national hazard mapping to guide proactive mitigation, including fuel management, land-use planning, infrastructure protection, and evacuation routing. However, process-based wildfire simulation frameworks (e.g., BurnP3 and BurnP3+) rely on computationally intensive Monte Carlo simulations to model burn probability, fire intensity, and rate of spread. These workflows can take days to weeks to process a single regional modelling unit. To overcome these computational bottlenecks, we present three contributions developed through collaboration between AI researchers and wildfire modelling experts: (a) a standardized framework for training, fine-tuning, and evaluating AI surrogate models against process-based wildfire simulators; (b) a multi-task deep learning surrogate trained on national-scale data to emulate burn probability, mean fire intensity, and mean rate of spread at a fraction of the computational cost (seconds); and (c) domain-specific metrics and counterfactual evaluation protocols to probe out-of-distribution generalization. Integrating geospatial data (fuel, terrain, ignition likelihood) and regional weather, our model approximates BurnP3+ simulation outputs, achieving strong performance across agreement, rank-correlation, error, and spatial-overlap metrics. It preserves downstream hazard classifications and produces physically plausible responses to expert-informed counterfactual interventions. On a representative region, the surrogate achieves 806-fold end-to-end CPU acceleration and uses 13% of BurnP3+'s host memory, facilitating rapid scenario analysis.

articles.title: ULME: Predictive Coupling for Mutually Reinforcing Embedding and Language Modeling
articles.content: Text embedding and text generation are two of the most useful capabilities of modern large language models, yet they are typically provided by separate specialized models (an embedder and a generator) trained with incompatible objectives and deployed side by side in retrieval-augmented generation and agent systems. Recent unified embedding-generation models such as GritLM share parameters between the two capabilities, but they either switch attention regimes between modes or optimize embedding and language modeling as parallel objectives that never supervise each other. We argue that these designs are only partially unified: the two capabilities coexist on the same weights, but do not shape each other. We propose ULME, a post-training framework that unifies embedding and language modeling on a causal decoder-only LLM through predictive coupling. ULME inserts a chain of learnable slots between the query and the answer, reads a semantic embedding and a reasoning embedding from two designated slots, and trains three objectives on a shared causal backbone: a contrastive loss anchoring the semantic slot to document representations, a language-modeling loss supervising answer generation, and a stop-gradient predictive loss that aligns the reasoning slot with a pooled summary of the answer, so that generation actively shapes what the embedding encodes. Across two model families (Qwen2.5, Qwen3) and eight scales spanning 0.5B-8B parameters, a single ULME checkpoint improves MTEB by 3.3-4.1 points over the strongest open-source baseline, tightens BRIGHT and AdvBench-IR simultaneously, and remains on par with a generation-only fine-tune on standard accuracy benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, HumanEval), demonstrating that genuine unification yields mutually reinforcing rather than merely coexisting capabilities.
articles.summary: ULME는 인과적 디코더 모델 하나에서 텍스트 임베딩과 생성을 상호 보완적으로 학습하는 사후학습 프레임워크다. 질문과 답변 사이의 학습 가능한 슬롯에 의미·추론 표현을 배치하고, 대조학습·언어모델링·답변 요약 예측 목적을 연결해 생성 학습이 임베딩 표현에도 영향을 주도록 했다. Qwen 계열의 0.5B~8B 모델 실험에서 비교한 최상위 오픈소스 기준보다 MTEB가 3.3~4.1점 높으면서 주요 생성 평가 성능을 유지해, 검색과 생성 모델을 별도로 운영하는 시스템의 통합 가능성을 제시했다.

articles.title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models
articles.content: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer clinical questions about medical images, but trustworthy use requires visual grounding: models should localize the pathology they report rather than rely on spurious shortcuts. Whether MLLMs can visually ground clinical findings in retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), the most widely used imaging modality in ophthalmology, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RetinaGroundBench, the first benchmark for biomarker visual grounding in retinal OCT. It comprises 815 B-scans exhaustively annotated by ophthalmologists with 4,537 bounding boxes covering 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases. Because MLLMs often fragment a single lesion into multiple partial predictions, we propose AggIoU, a metric that evaluates whether the union of overlapping predicted boxes covers the annotated region. Across 27 open-source MLLMs (0.8-38B parameters), we find that visual grounding remains largely unsolved: the best general-purpose model achieves a macro F1 of just 23.7%, with consistently low recall, despite reaching up to 73% balanced accuracy on biomarker presence questions. To narrow this gap, we developed RetGrounder, an MLLM fine-tuned using an OCT-specific strategy integrating grounding and textual information. Despite its relatively small size (8B), RetGrounder improves grounding F1 to 33.9%, a 43% relative improvement. Our benchmark provides a reference point for measuring progress in the field of OCT diagnosis with MLLMs.
articles.summary: RetinaGroundBench는 망막 OCT 영상에서 멀티모달 언어모델이 병변의 존재를 답하는 것뿐 아니라 실제 위치까지 찾는지 평가하는 벤치마크다. 안과 전문의가 주석한 영상 815장과 경계상자 4,537개로 오픈소스 모델 27개를 평가한 결과, 최상위 범용 모델의 위치 식별 매크로 F1은 23.7%에 그쳐 병변 존재 질문의 정확도와 큰 차이를 보였다. OCT 특화 학습을 적용한 8B RetGrounder는 F1을 33.9%로 높였지만, 결과는 의료 영상 설명 능력을 시각적 근거 확보 능력과 별도로 검증해야 함을 시사한다.

articles.title: You.com Launches Inference Router: 12 Open-Weight Models With 99.9% Uptime SLA
articles.content: You.com has launched Inference Router, a managed API for running open-weight models in production. The You.com Inference Router is an OpenAI-compatible service that routes requests across 12 live models. It bundles a 99.9% minimum uptime SLA and zero data retention (ZDR). It adds 100% US hosting and server-side web search. It is pay-as-you-go, with no platform fee. TL;DR Size: 12 live models, from GPT-OSS 120B (125K context) to Kimi K3 and Qwen3.8 Max (1M context). Kimi K3 is a 2.8T-parameter model; Qwen3.8 Max is a 2.4T MoE. Runs on: Fully managed. Requests hit You.com Inference Direct first, then fail over to US-hosted partners. No GPUs to manage. Performance: On You.com’s LiveNewsBench run, open-weight models plus You.com search matched frontier models at lower cost. Best: GLM-5.3 with You.com search scored 86.53%, at $0.0485 per question versus $0.0920 for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (self-reported). Worst: Per-token prices sit near market. Kimi K3 is $2.85/$14.25, only 5% below Together AI’s $3.00/$15.00. What is You.com Inference Router? It is one API for many open-weight models. The endpoint is https://api.you.com, with OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible routes. Existing SDK code moves over by changing the base URL and key. You.com team frames the problem around stalled migrations. Dev teams test open-weight models on aggregators, then hit security review. Reviewers ask about ZDR, US hosting, access controls and DPAs. Dedicated providers clear those bars, but usually with a large commitment. Inference Router targets that gap. How does the routing and failover work? Every request goes first to You.com Inference Direct, the company’s own inference capacity. If it is down or full, the request fails over to a vetted partner. The official post names Parasail, Wafer, Alibaba Cloud, Meta and Inception, with Prime Intellect coming soon. All are 100% US-hosted and must meet ZDR rules. Failover does not change the bill. Each model has 1 published per-token price. You.com also offers spend caps per API key and daily usage views by model, cost and provider. Accounts run on SOC 2 compliant infrastructure, with a DPA on request. What does zero data retention cover? The ZDR policy states that prompts and outputs are processed in memory and not stored. It covers both model calls and web search requests. You.com keeps only operational metadata, such as token counts, timestamps and account IDs. Prompt hashes, de-identified text and disk-backed prompt caches are explicitly excluded. Which models are available, and what do they cost? The models page lists 12 live models, all US-hosted. Prices are per 1M tokens (input / output): Kimi K3 (Moonshot AI): $2.85 / $14.25, 1M context Qwen3.8 Max (Alibaba): $1.85 / $5.55, 1M context GLM 5.3 (Z.ai): $1.35 / $4.25, 1M context DeepSeek V4 Pro: $1.65 / $3.65, 1M context DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: $0.30 / $1.20, 1M context Mercury 3 (Inception): $0.10 / $0.35, 1M context GPT-OSS 120B (OpenAI): $0.097 / $0.73, 125K context Muse Wonder, Muse Spark 1.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, Qwen3.8 Flash and MiniMax M3 round out the list. How does built-in web search work? Developers declare a web_search or web_extract tool, and the router runs searches for the model. The docs show up to 20 results per search and a default of 30 search rounds. Responses return a web_results object with citations. Search runs on the same server as the model. You.com says internal tests show up to 15% lower latency.
